content: 1. The administration of the BCG vaccine should be deferred until the patient's immune status has been thoroughly evaluated. 2. There is no specific FDA guidance regarding the use of the BCG vaccine in relation to gender-specific populations. 3. There is no specific FDA guidance regarding the use of the BCG vaccine in relation to racial populations. 4. There is no specific FDA guidance regarding the use of the BCG vaccine in patients with renal impairment. 5. There is no specific FDA guidance regarding the use of the BCG vaccine in patients with hepatic impairment. 6. There is no specific FDA guidance regarding the use of the BCG vaccine in women of reproductive potential or in males. 7. There is no specific FDA guidance regarding the use of the BCG vaccine in immunocompromised patients. 8. The preparation of the BCG vaccine suspension must be performed using aseptic techniques. 9. To prevent cross-contamination, parenteral drugs should not be prepared in areas where the BCG vaccine has been prepared. 10. A separate area is recommended for the preparation of the BCG vaccine suspension. 11. All equipment, supplies, and receptacles that come into contact with the BCG vaccine should be handled and disposed of as biohazardous materials. 12. The pharmacist or individual responsible for mixing the vaccine should wear gloves and take precautions to avoid contact of the BCG vaccine with broken skin. 13. 14. Using aseptic methods, 1 mL of sterile water for injection (USP) at 4–25°C (39–77°F) should be added to one vial of the vaccine for adult use. 15. The vial should be gently swirled until a homogeneous suspension is achieved. Forceful agitation should be avoided to prevent clumping of the mycobacteria. 16. Individuals administering the vaccine should take necessary precautions to minimize the risk of spreading disease. 17. Hands should be washed before attending to each new patient. 18. Syringes and needles used for vaccine administration must be sterile and preferably disposable to minimize the risk of contamination. 19. A separate needle and syringe should be used for each application. 20. Disposable needles and the multiple puncture device should be discarded as biohazardous waste in labeled, puncture-proof containers to prevent accidental needlestick injuries or reuse. 21. After use, any unused vaccine and all materials exposed to the product should be immediately placed in a biohazard container and disposed of appropriately. 22. Reconstituted vaccine should be kept refrigerated, protected from direct sunlight, and used within 2 hours. Freezing of the reconstituted product is not recommended. 23. The contents of the BCG vaccine vial should not be filtered. 24. Precautions should be taken to avoid exposing the BCG vaccine to direct sunlight. 25. Bacteriostatic solutions must be avoided during preparation. 26. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration, whenever the solution and container permit. 27. Reconstitution should result in a uniform suspension of the bacilli. 28. BCG vaccination is reserved for individuals who exhibit a reaction of less than 5 mm induration after skin testing with 5 TU of PPD tuberculin. 29. The preferred method of skin testing is the Mantoux tuberculin skin test using 0.1 mL of 5 tuberculin units (TU) of PPD. 30. It is recommended that a Mantoux skin test be performed prior to BCG vaccination to confirm the absence of tuberculosis infection. 31. The vaccine should be administered only after fully explaining the risks and benefits to the vaccinee, parent, or guardian. 32. BCG vaccination should not be given to individuals previously infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. 33. The vaccine is administered percutaneously using a sterile multiple puncture device. 34. The multiple puncture device consists of a plastic holder for a thin, wafer-like stainless steel plate (7/8 by 1 1/8) with 36 protruding points. 35. After the vaccine is prepared, the skin site should be cleansed with an alcohol or acetone sponge and allowed to dry thoroughly. 36. There is limited information available regarding the monitoring of the BCG vaccine in the drug label. 37. There is limited information available regarding the IV compatibility of the BCG vaccine in the drug label. 38. Accidental overdoses, if treated immediately with anti-tuberculous drugs, have not led to complications. 39. If the vaccination response is allowed to progress, it can still be successfully treated with anti-tuberculous drugs, but complications may include regional adenitis, lupus vulgaris, subcutaneous cold abscesses, ocular lesions, and others. 40. The BCG vaccine for percutaneous use is an attenuated, live culture preparation of the Bacillus of Calmette and Guérin (BCG) strain of Mycobacterium bovis. 41. The TICE® strain used in this BCG vaccine preparation was developed at the University of Illinois from a strain originally obtained from the Pasteur Institute. 42. The medium used to grow the TICE® BCG organism for the preparation of the freeze-dried cake contains glycerin, asparagine, citric acid, potassium phosphate, magnesium sulfate, and iron ammonium citrate. 43. The final preparation prior to freeze-drying also contains lactose. 44. The freeze-dried BCG preparation is delivered in vials, each containing 1 to 8 × 10^8 colony-forming units (CFU) of BCG, equivalent to approximately 50 mg wet weight. 45. Determination of in-vitro potency is achieved through colony counts derived from a serial dilution assay. 46. 47. Reconstitution requires the addition of sterile water for injection (USP) at 4–25°C (39–77°F). 48. For adult dosage, 1 mL of sterile water for injection (USP) should be added to one vial of vaccine. 49. For pediatric dosage, 2 mL of sterile water for injection (USP) should be added to one vial of vaccine. 50. No preservatives have been added to the vaccine. 51. Tuberculosis (TB) is primarily an airborne communicable disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. 52. Tuberculosis is a significant global public health issue, with an estimated 8–10 million cases and 2–3 million deaths occurring annually. 53. The control of TB in the United States has been a persistent challenge, particularly with the resurgence of TB in the late 1980s and early 1990s. 54. In the United States, TB incidence had declined approximately 6% per year since nationwide reporting began in 1953. 55. However, in 1985, there was a 1.1% increase in TB cases compared to the previous year. 56. This upward trend continued through 1992, when the incidence was 10.5 cases per 100,000 population. 57. In 1993, there was a 5.2% decrease in TB cases compared to 1992, with a rate of 9.8 cases per 100,000 population. 58. By 1997, the total number of reported TB cases was 19,855, or 7.4 cases per 100,000 people. 59. This incidence rate represented the fifth consecutive year of declining TB cases and a 26% decrease since the peak in 1992. 60. In the 1990s, drug-resistant TB also became a significant public health concern. 61. During the period of 1993–1996 in the United States, 13.1% of TB patients were infected with TB strains resistant to at least one first-line treatment drug (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol).
